sections.label: MinLaw accepts Committee recommendations
sections.summary: MinLaw accepted 12 of the Committee's 15 recommendations and worked with industry and VWOs to implement them progressively.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: MinLaw accepted 12 of the Committee's 15 recommendations and has worked with the industry and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) to implement them progressively.

sections.label: Aggregate borrowing cap for individuals
sections.summary: It sets an overall limit on what an individual can borrow from all licensed moneylenders combined, with proposed caps of $3,000 and six times monthly income.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: It sets an overall limit on the amount an individual can borrow from all licensed moneylenders, combined.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: We intend to set an aggregate cap of $3,000 for individuals with an annual income below $20,000, and a cap of six times' the monthly income for all other individuals, as recommended by ACML.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Between March 2016 and March 2017, less than 2% of Singaporean borrowers who took out loans have an outstanding balance exceeding the cap.

sections.label: Credit report before granting loans
sections.summary: The Bill introduces a new section 30N requiring moneylenders to obtain a borrower's credit report from MLCB before granting any loan.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: The Bill introduces a new section 30N, which requires moneylenders to obtain a borrower’s credit report from MLCB before granting any loan.

sections.label: Offence for breaching interest caps
sections.summary: The Bill makes it an offence for a moneylender to enter a loan contract breaching interest caps, punishable by fine and/or imprisonment, and makes such contracts unenforceable.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Under the Bill, it will be an offence for a moneylender to enter into a loan contract that breaches the caps on interest or late interest, which will be punishable by a fine of up to $20,000 and/or imprisonment of up to six months.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: The Bill also makes such a loan contract unenforceable, and any guarantee or money paid out by the moneylender under the contract will not be recoverable in any Court of law.

sections.label: Prescribed amount of $100,000
sections.summary: Following ACML's recommendation, this amount will be prescribed at $100,000.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Following the recommendation of ACML, this amount will be prescribed at $100,000.

sections.label: Drop in moneylender complaints
sections.summary: Complaints against licensed moneylenders dropped from 271 in 2012 to 104 in 2017, a reduction of more than 60%.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Complaints against licensed moneylenders have dropped from 271 in 2012 to 104 in 2017, a reduction of more than 60%.

sections.label: Moneylending borrowing amounts 2015 2016
sections.summary: In 2016, about 40,000 borrowers borrowed $367 million, up from $239 million for 35,000 borrowers a year earlier.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: In 2016, it was tabulated that $367 million was borrowed by close to 40,000 borrowers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: A year before that, the amount was $239 million for 35,000 borrowers.

sections.label: Moneylender shareholding approval and registration
sections.summary: Approval before shareholding changes would block unsavoury characters, and a question asks measures for the remaining one-third of moneylenders to register as companies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Likewise, getting approval before increasing shareholding or becoming a shareholder will put the brakes on unsavoury characters entering into this industry.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: We have about 160 licensed moneylenders in Singapore and more than 100 of them have registered themselves as companies, whereby they are required to submit annual audited accounts to the Registrar.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: I would, however, like to ask the Senior Minister of State what are the measures being taken to get the remaining one-third of moneylenders to comply and register?

sections.label: Moneylender debt recovery agents intimidation
sections.summary: Questions ask how many moneylenders use own or third-party debt recovery agents and how many intimidation cases were reported or prosecuted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: How many moneylenders employ their own debt recovery agents and how many make use of third-party debt recovery companies?

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: How many cases of intimidation have been prosecuted or reported?

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: While we also need to protect the interests of honest moneylenders dealing with difficult clients, we must also similarly ensure that less than scrupulous moneylenders do not intimidate vulnerable clients.

sections.label: Unlicensed moneylending cases decline
sections.summary: Since the Moneylenders Act, unlicensed moneylending cases fell from over 18,000 in 2009 to 4,862 in 2015, with arrests falling to around 1,500.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, since the Moneylenders Act was enacted, unlicensed moneylending has been brought under control from its heyday in 2009 of over 18,000 cases.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Minister updated this House in August 2016 that unlicensed moneylending cases fell to a 10-year low in 2015, at 4,862 cases.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The number of people arrested for unlicensed moneylending activities also fell to around 1,500 in 2015 from close to 2,000 in 2011.

sections.label: Ministry accepted Committee recommendations
sections.summary: The Ministry accepted 12 of the 15 recommendations advised by the Committee and implemented them in late 2015.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Ministry accepted 12 of the 15 recommendations advised by the Committee and implemented them in late 2015.

sections.label: Contract standardisation and peer-to-peer lending
sections.summary: Standardisation is limited to contract forms with flexible terms, moneylenders innovate contracts for predatory practices, and peer-to-peer lending platforms are rising.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If I am not mistaken, standardisation is currently limited to the standard form used for contracts, which still allows for very flexible contracting terms within the interest rate and borrowing caps.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Also, moneylenders have been innovating contracts to sustain predatory practices, and the Registry has been issuing directions and advisories with the burden placed on consumers to monitor and report.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Fourth and lastly, peer-to-peer lending platforms are on the rise around the world and is one exciting bright spot for innovation in financial technology (fintech).

sections.label: P2P lending and moneylender law
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the law is adequate to tackle P2P lending platforms becoming de facto moneylenders, and warns against over-regulation driving borrowers to unlicensed moneylenders.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Is the law currently adequate to tackle the potential issue of P2P lending platforms becoming de facto moneylenders in practice?

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: My concern is that in the pursuit of good intentions, the Government might be over-tightening, over-regulating, thus shutting out individual borrowers from access to credit lines and driving them to unlicensed moneylenders.

sections.label: Moneylending share of consumer lending
sections.summary: Moneylending is often not considered a mainstream financial service and makes up less than 1% of overall consumer lending in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It is often not even considered a mainstream financial service.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It makes up less than 1% of overall consumer lending in Singapore.

sections.label: Borrower numbers, amounts and industry objectives
sections.summary: Borrower numbers and amounts borrowed rose from 2014 to 2016, and the speaker lists five objectives for planning the industry.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In 2014, 2015 and 2016, the numbers of borrowers increased from 31,000 to 35,000 and 40,000 respectively.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In the same three year span, the amount borrowed moved up from $239 million to $282 million and $367 million.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In planning and strategising for this industry the important necessary objectives we want should be to: (a) prevent individuals from borrowing beyond their means; (b) stabilise the industry; (c) improve the rates of debt repayment from licensed lenders; (d) reduce and deter borrowing from unlicensed lenders; and (e) professionalise and increase the transparency and accountability throughout the industry.

sections.label: Overdue unsecured debt and delinquent debtors
sections.summary: In 2015 the Straits Times reported 85,352 consumers with overdue unsecured debt of $288.4 million, and the Credit Card Bureau reported 101,493 delinquent debtors.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In 2015, the Straits Times reported that 85,352 Singapore consumers have overdue unsecured debt totalling $288.4 million.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Credit Card Bureau also revealed that, in the same year, the total number of delinquent debtors hit 101,493, a significant increase from just over 73,000 in 2011.

sections.label: Gambling addicts and moneylending firms
sections.summary: NAMS reported a doubling of gambling addicts seeking help since 2010, and the speaker calls for cooperation between NCPG and registered moneylending firms.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In 2015, the National Addiction Management Service (NAMS) reported a doubling in the number of gambling addicts seeking help since 2010.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It is good news that more people are seeking avenues to quit their gambling addiction.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I would call for closer cooperation between the National Council on Problem Gambling (NCPG) and registered moneylending firms, to help NCPG better identify and reach out to gambling addicts.

sections.label: Bill's aggregate loan cap
sections.summary: The Bill aims to restrict how much people can borrow from licensed moneylenders by introducing an aggregate loan cap depending on income levels.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Amongst other things, this Bill aims to restrict the amount people are able to borrow from licensed moneylenders, by introducing an aggregate loan cap depending on income levels.

sections.label: Debt collector training and interest cap
sections.summary: The speaker suggests SkillsFuture courses for debt collectors and supports clauses 13 and 14 capping interest on borrowed amounts.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I am sure there could even be SkillsFuture courses on how such skills and ethics can be trained and nurtured for debt collectors.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I also support clauses 13 and 14 which make amendments to sections 22 and 22A respectively, where a cap is placed on the amount of interest imposed on the amount borrowed.

sections.label: Private company maintaining borrower records
sections.summary: The speaker questions why an approved private moneylending company, not a MOF or MAS body, maintains borrower records under section 30E.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: While section 30E makes provisions for a record of borrowing, similar to the Credit Bureau Report, to be made available for each borrower who borrows from moneylending companies, I do question why an approved moneylending company, which is still a private entity, is the one appointed to maintain such records of borrowers.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Why is a regulatory body overseen by the Ministry of Finance (MOF) or the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) not tasked to do so instead?

sections.label: Foreign licence revocation unsuitability
sections.summary: A person is deemed unsuitable for moneylending if their foreign moneylending licence was withdrawn, cancelled or revoked abroad.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: One basis upon which an individual would be deemed unsuitable to take part in the moneylending business is where they had carried out moneylending business in a foreign country for which the licence has been withdrawn, cancelled or revoked by an authority in the foreign country.

sections.label: Licensees' data breach notification gap
sections.summary: The speaker notes licensees lack the same obligation as MLCB to notify the Registrar of events compromising data confidentiality or security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: While the provisions impose duties on the use and disclosure of borrowers' information and duties to maintain confidentiality and security on licensees and MLCB, I notice that licensees are not under the same obligation as MLCB to notify the Registrar of events that compromise the confidentiality or security of its data.

sections.label: Public agency access to information
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether information is available to anyone in a public agency or only those needing it for policy formulation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Would the information be available to anyone within the public agency, or only the individuals or departments requiring the information for policy formulation?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This is of concern, especially because public agencies which are specified in the Personal Data Protection (Statutory Bodies) Notification 2013 are excluded from data protection obligations in PDPA 2012.

sections.label: ACML debt collection guidelines review
sections.summary: The Ministry said it will later review ACML recommendations to create guidelines for acceptable debt collection practices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: On the recommendations of the ACML which formed the bases for these amendments, the Ministry had indicated that it will review the recommendations to create guidelines for acceptable debt collection practices at a later stage.

sections.label: Outstanding loans and borrowers rise
sections.summary: Outstanding loans rose from $239 million in 2014 to $282 million in 2015 and $367 million in 2016, with borrowers rising from 31,000 to 40,000.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In 2016, outstanding loans totalled $367 million, an increase of 30% from $282 million in 2015, which was also up from $239 million in 2014.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Correspondingly, the number of borrowers went up to 40,000 in 2016, from 35,000 in 2015 and 31,000 in 2014.

sections.label: Borrowers exceeding income multiple decline
sections.summary: Borrowers with outstanding unsecured debt over 18 times monthly income fell 47% to 27,000, from 51,000 in 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: The number of borrowers with outstanding unsecured debt exceeding 18 times their monthly income has declined by 47% to 27,000 borrowers, compared to 2015 where there were 51,000 people in that situation.

sections.label: Moneylender loan disclosure condition proposed
sections.summary: The question asks whether the Ministry could require registered moneylenders to fully disclose total loan plus interest on websites and advertisements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Could the Ministry consider imposing a condition requiring all registered moneylenders to provide a full disclosure on the total amount of loan plus interest to be paid, for example, on their websites and advertisements?

sections.label: Singaporean borrowers exceeding income cap
sections.summary: Nearly 2% of Singaporean borrowers who took loans between March 2016 and March 2017 will have an outstanding balance exceeding the income cap.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Among Singaporean borrowers who took out loans between March 2016 and March 2017, nearly 2% will have an outstanding balance exceeding the income cap.

sections.label: Moneylender borrowers in third quarter 2017
sections.summary: As at the third quarter of 2017, around 41,000 individuals borrowed from moneylenders, about 80% citizens and permanent residents, with $339 million outstanding.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: As at the third quarter of 2017, around 41,000 individuals borrowed from moneylenders, and around 80% of these were Singaporean Citizens and Permanent Residents subject to regulatory loan caps.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Their total outstanding loan amount was $339 million.

sections.label: Unlicensed moneylending reports and arrests
sections.summary: In 2016 there were 550 reports of unlicensed moneylending to the Police and 1,100 persons arrested that year.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In response to Assoc Prof Daniel Goh’s query on the number of unlicensed moneylending cases reported and the number of offenders arrested, there were 550 reports of unlicensed moneylending to the Police in 2016, while 1,100 persons were arrested in that same year.

sections.label: Moneylender advertising restrictions
sections.summary: Licensed moneylenders may advertise only on their business premises, own websites and business or consumer directories.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Under the Registrar’s Directions on Advertising issued on 31 July 2013, licensed moneylenders are only allowed to advertise on the facades of their approved places of business, their own Internet websites and business or consumer directories in print or online media.

sections.label: Penalties for moneylender offences
sections.summary: Non-compliance and collusion with unlicensed moneylenders carry fines, imprisonment, licence revocation and caning.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Failure to comply is punishable by a fine of $20,000 and/or imprisonment of up to six months.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Any licensed moneylender found to have colluded with an unlicensed moneylender by passing on customer information will have his licence revoked and will be prosecuted under the Moneylenders Act.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Such behaviour is punishable under the Act by a fine of between $30,000 and $300,000 for individuals and between $50,000 and $500,000 for bodies corporate, as well as up to six strokes of the cane for a first-time offence and up to 12 strokes of the cane for subsequent offences.

sections.label: Borrower information sharing prohibition
sections.summary: Section 30Q prohibits moneylenders from sharing borrower information except with MLCB, the Registrar and their own employees.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: As to Dr Intan Mokhtar's query on the sharing of borrower information, section 30Q of the amended Act prohibits moneylenders from sharing borrower information with anyone else besides MLCB, the Registrar and its own employees in the course of their work.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This means that an individual's banks and employers, or any moneylender that he has not approached for a loan, will not be able to access his credit report unless he chooses to provide it.

sections.label: Verification process penalties and credit report fee
sections.summary: Failure to abide by the verification process is punishable by a fine and/or imprisonment, and the 50-cent credit report fee is unlikely to deter due diligence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Failure to abide by this verification process is punishable by a fine of $20,000 and/or imprisonment of up to six months.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Given the penalties, to answer Mr Alex Yam’s query, the nominal fee of 50 cents per credit report is unlikely to deter moneylenders from conducting due diligence before lending.

sections.label: Independent audits of licensees
sections.summary: Section 24A requires all licensees to conduct independent audits and submit audited financial statements to the Registrar yearly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In addition to the Registrar’s regular audits, section 24A of the amended Act requires all licensees to conduct independent audits of the licensees' accounts and to submit those audited financial statements to the Registrar every year.

sections.label: Reasons for rejected licence applications
sections.summary: There is no statutory right of appeal, but the Registrar will give rejected applicants reasons for the rejection.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Even though there is no statutory right of appeal available for a rejected applicant, the Registrar will provide the rejected applicant with reasons for the rejection.

sections.label: Reports received by Registry
sections.summary: The Registry received 124 reports in 2016, and this number dropped to 104 in 2017.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In 2016, 124 reports were received by the Registry, and this number dropped to 104 in 2017.

sections.label: New section 6A licence capital
sections.summary: The Bill introduces section 6A, providing that only a company with the prescribed paid-up capital may hold a licence after the appointed day.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Bill introduces a new section 6A, which provides that only a company with the prescribed paid-up capital may hold a licence after the appointed day.

sections.label: Standardising loan products recommendation
sections.summary: MinLaw amended the Moneylenders Rules in 2015 to mandate that all loan contracts provide for equal instalments at equal intervals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: As for the recommendation on standardising loan products, MinLaw took in the recommendation and amended the Moneylenders Rules in 2015 to mandate that all loan contracts provide for payment of equal instalments at equal intervals of time, to facilitate comparison of loan packages.

sections.label: Protecting borrowers and mystery shoppers
sections.summary: MinLaw will work with agencies and stakeholders to protect borrowers, and a mystery shopper approach was suggested to prove information sharing.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: MinLaw will continue to work with other agencies and stakeholders to protect individual borrowers while maintaining their access to credit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: On this issue of sharing of information from a licenced to an unlicensed moneylender, because they can just pass a sheet of paper at the coffee shop, it is very difficult to prove.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: So, may I suggest to the regulator, they consider having what we call "mystery shopper"?

sentences.speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
sentences.text: That means we get somebody to approach a licensed moneylender and, if soon after that, that person receives an SMS, and if it is proven through multiple mystery shoppers who approached this person, then we have circumstantial grounds to charge that the moneylender is, indeed, passing on information.
